VI.1.title: Fit to face south
VI.1.reflection: Confucius says Ran Yong could sit facing south, the position of a ruler. Yong then asks about Zisang Bozi, whom the Master calls easy-going. Yong distinguishes: being easy in small matters while serious within is acceptable; being easy within and easy in practice is too much. The Master agrees with him.
VI.1.question: Where in your work is ease a strength, and where is it carelessness?

VI.2.title: He did not shift his anger
VI.2.reflection: Duke Ai asks which disciple loved learning. Yan Hui did: he did not shift his anger onto others, and he did not make the same mistake twice. He died young, and there is no one like him now. Love of learning is described entirely as conduct.
VI.2.question: When did you last take out on someone an anger that was about something else?

VI.3.title: Not adding to the rich
VI.3.reflection: Ran Qiu asks grain for the mother of Gongxi Chi, who has gone on a mission, and gives far more than the Master named; Chi travels with fat horses and fine furs. The junzi helps those in need, not those already well off. Then Yuan Si, made steward, refuses his salary, and Confucius tells him to accept it and give it to his neighbours.
VI.3.question: Do you give more easily where it is seen, or where it is needed?

VI.4.title: The calf of a brindled cow
VI.4.reflection: Speaking of Ran Yong, whose father was of low standing, Confucius says: if the calf of a plough ox is red and well horned, even if people would not use it, would the spirits of the hills and rivers refuse it? Worth is not inherited and not cancelled by birth.
VI.4.question: Where have you judged someone by where they came from?

VI.5.title: Three months
VI.5.reflection: Hui's heart did not depart from ren for three months together; the others reach it for a day or a month, and no more. The chapter treats goodness as something sustained over time, measured in months and days.
VI.5.question: How long can you keep a good intention before it lapses?

VI.6.title: Fit for office
VI.6.reflection: Ji Kangzi asks whether Zilu, Zigong and Ran Qiu could hold office. Zilu is decisive, Zigong perceptive, Ran Qiu versatile: what difficulty would they have? Office, unlike ren, the Master grants readily.
VI.6.question: What is your one strength that would make you fit for a task?

VI.7.title: Refusing the post
VI.7.reflection: The Ji family asks Min Ziqian to govern Bi. Decline for me politely, he says, and if they ask again, I will be across the river Wen, out of the state. He refuses to serve a family that has usurped power, and he refuses with courtesy.
VI.7.question: Have you ever refused an offer for a reason you kept to yourself?

VI.8.title: Through the window
VI.8.reflection: Boniu is gravely ill. Confucius visits and holds his hand through the window. "It is fate. That such a man should have such an illness!" he says twice. The scene is one of the most personal in the book, grief without explanation.
VI.8.question: How do you stay with someone when there is nothing to be done?

VI.9.title: One basket, one gourd
VI.9.reflection: A basket of rice, a gourd of water, a mean lane: others could not bear the hardship, and Hui did not let it change his joy. Worthy indeed was Hui. The praise begins and ends with the same words, as if the Master could not say it once.
VI.9.question: What joy of yours does not depend on comfort?

VI.10.title: Drawing the line
VI.10.reflection: Ran Qiu says it is not that he does not love the Way, but his strength is not enough. Those whose strength fails collapse halfway, Confucius answers, but you are drawing a line in advance. The limit he describes is not exhaustion but a decision.
VI.10.question: Where have you drawn a line before reaching it?
VI.10.exercise: Take one thing you have decided you cannot do and do the first small part of it today.

VI.11.title: A scholar of which kind
VI.11.reflection: Confucius tells Zixia to be a ru of the junzi kind, not of the small man's kind. Ru later became the name of the whole Confucian school; here it means a man of learning. The warning is that learning alone does not decide what kind of person one is.
VI.11.question: What kind of learned person do you want to be?

VI.12.title: Never a short cut
VI.12.reflection: Ziyou, governor of Wucheng, is asked if he has found good people. One, Tantai Mieming, never takes a short cut when walking and never comes to the governor's house except on public business. Two small habits, and they say everything about his integrity.
VI.12.question: What small habit of yours would tell a stranger the most about you?

VI.13.title: My horse would not go
VI.13.reflection: Meng Zhifan did not boast. Covering the retreat after a defeat, he whipped his horse as they reached the gate and said he had not dared to be last, his horse just would not go faster. He turns his courage into a joke about his horse.
VI.13.question: How do you take credit, when you have earned it?

VI.14.title: Glib and handsome
VI.14.reflection: Without the glib tongue of Tuo the priest and the good looks of Song Zhao, Confucius says, it is hard to get by in this age. It is bitter. The two men were famous for winning favour with talk and with beauty.
VI.14.question: What qualities does your own age reward that it should not?

VI.15.title: Out by the door
VI.15.reflection: Who can leave a house except by the door? Why then does no one go by this Way? The Way is as obvious as the door, and still people climb out of windows.
VI.15.question: What obvious door are you avoiding?

VI.16.title: Substance and refinement
VI.16.reflection: When substance outweighs refinement, a person is rustic; when refinement outweighs substance, they are like a clerk. Only when the two are balanced is there a junzi. Neither raw honesty nor polish is enough alone.
VI.16.question: Which do you have more of, substance or refinement?

VI.17.title: Born upright
VI.17.reflection: People are born upright; one who lives without uprightness escapes by luck. Legge reads it as a claim about human nature, an early hint of the later debate about whether nature is good. It is also simply a warning.
VI.17.question: Do you think people are born upright, or become so?

VI.18.title: Knowing, loving, delighting
VI.18.reflection: Knowing something is not as good as loving it; loving it is not as good as delighting in it. Three degrees of relation to the same thing, each closer than the last.
VI.18.question: What do you know, what do you love, and what do you delight in?

VI.19.title: Teaching to the level
VI.19.reflection: To those above the middle one can speak of higher things; to those below, not. It sounds hierarchical and is mostly practical: teaching must meet the learner where they are. The book shows Confucius doing this again and again, giving different answers to the same question.
VI.19.question: When have you explained something above or below the level of the person in front of you?

VI.20.title: Wisdom and the spirits
VI.20.reflection: Fan Chi asks about wisdom: devote yourself to what is right for the people, respect the spirits and keep them at a distance. About ren: put the hard work first and the reward after. Both answers point toward the human and the present.
VI.20.question: Do you more often think of the reward before the work, or after?

VI.21.title: Water and mountains
VI.21.reflection: The wise delight in water, the humane in mountains; the wise are active, the humane still; the wise are joyful, the humane long-lived. The pairing is poetic, not a rule: two temperaments, each true in its way.
VI.21.question: Are you more drawn to water or to mountains?

VI.22.title: One change
VI.22.reflection: With one change Qi could reach the level of Lu; with one change Lu could reach the Way. Lu was the home of the Zhou rites, Qi the more powerful state. Confucius sees reform as close, just one step away in each case.
VI.22.question: What one change would bring something you care about to where it should be?

VI.23.title: A gu that is not a gu
VI.23.reflection: A gu was a ritual drinking vessel, named for its corners. A gu that is not a gu: what a gu, what a gu! The things have changed and the names remain. It is the setting of names right, zhengming, without the word.
VI.23.question: What word do you still use for something that no longer matches it?

VI.24.title: A man in the well
VI.24.reflection: Zai Wo tests the Master: if a humane person were told someone had fallen into a well, would he jump in after them? Why would he? The junzi can be made to go to the well, not to throw himself in; he can be deceived, not made a fool of. Goodness is not the same as stupidity.
VI.24.question: When has someone used your goodness against your judgement?

VI.25.title: Broad learning, held by ritual
VI.25.reflection: The junzi studies widely in culture and draws it together with ritual, and so does not go astray. Breadth needs a binding, or it scatters.
VI.25.question: What holds together everything you have learned?

VI.26.title: The visit to Nanzi
VI.26.reflection: Confucius visits Nanzi, the wife of the ruler of Wei, a woman with a scandalous name. Zilu is displeased, and the Master swears: if I have done wrong, may Heaven reject me. The book keeps a moment where the teacher must defend himself to his student.
VI.26.question: When have you had to defend yourself to someone who expected better of you?

VI.27.title: The constant mean
VI.27.reflection: The virtue of the mean, zhongyong, is the highest, and it has long been rare among the people. The phrase gave its name to a whole book, the Doctrine of the Mean, which this app keeps in Lore.
VI.27.question: Where in your life is the middle way the hardest to keep?

VI.28.title: Judging others by what is near
VI.28.reflection: Zigong imagines someone who benefits all the people; would that be ren? It would be sagehood, beyond what even Yao and Shun achieved. The humane person, wishing to be established, helps others be established; wishing to succeed, helps others succeed. To take what is near in oneself as the measure for others: that is the method of ren.
VI.28.question: What do you want for yourself that you could help someone else toward today?
